cards.title: AI is forcing us to pay off 40 years of technical debt

depth.text: AI helps security researchers find **old software bugs** that could become **server attacks**

A researcher at Calif, aided by AI tools, found a way to use PHP’s **out-of-memory bug** to run **arbitrary code** on a host server. Four engineers spent two months building a **patch**; commenters split over whether AI clears old debt or piles on **new debt**.

cards.camps: Two camps: Some say AI makes it cheaper to fix old code; others say it creates fresh debt and leaves developers trusting code they don’t understand.

comments.text: I hope some of these backdoors and/or 0-days being kept under wraps by nation states or corporate espionage companies (Pegasus et al) are being found incidentally through all this. It’s frustrating to have all these 0days and CVEs to patch for now, but in the long run perhaps we’ll leave with more robust software.

Is it forcing us to "pay off" technical debt or is it starting us on a compulsory endless treadmill of feature-neutral fix-work? Collectively, we just won't know for a while. It totally feels like the former if you watch it find and fix vulnerabilities or other debt-tasks one after another. But only so many of these "technical debt" issue are little off-by-one errors that get remedied by a…

I was down voted a lot months ago for saying that a lot of open source software had a false sense of being secure with the assumption that someone else would have audited the code. And this AI auditing is going to make the promise of open source software getting audited by others actually real. Nice to see others waking up to this reality.

While I have mixed feelings about AI's impact on my work, I am happy that I can address 5-7 years of technical debt in code bases as I come across it due to AI lowering the cost. Typically the solution is not too difficult; it just required a lot of time in research and testing which AI streamlined. I am able to verify everything at the end ran through the proper test cases and that the fix is…

I've been referring to this as honing a codebase (like a knife). I've used AI to vibecode sloppy one-off scripts, demos, and proof of concepts. But then I've turned around and used it to hammer in actual projects to a level of quality I just would not have had the time or motivation to achieve previously. That is a choice I make every day when I get into an argument with Claude about the chosen…

cards.title: Tell HN: Gemini trains on chat history, even for subscribers (personal accounts)

depth.text: someone found that **paying for Gemini** doesn't stop saved chats being used to **train AI**

With a personal Google AI subscription, saved chats can be used for training when **Keep Activity** is on, and a subset may be read by human reviewers. Turning it off stops training but means you lose chat sessions after **72 hours**; reviewed chats can be kept for **up to three years** even after activity is deleted.

retention of chats reviewed by humans

glossary.CI: Continuous integration: automatic checks that run when developers change code, helping catch problems early.
glossary.SSH key: A digital key your computer uses to prove it is allowed to connect to a service.
glossary.model weights: The learned settings inside an AI that shape how it responds.
glossary.3T-class: A label for a model with about three trillion learned settings; models that large can take lots of computing power to run.
glossary.context window: The amount of text and information an AI can take into account at one time.
glossary.multimodal: Able to work with more than one kind of input, such as text and images.
glossary.agentic model: An AI that can take steps toward completing a task, rather than only replying to a prompt.
glossary.benchmaxxed: A criticism that a model may be tuned to score well on tests without doing as well in everyday use.
glossary.value-free ideal: The belief that science should judge evidence without letting ethical or social concerns affect the judgment.
glossary.epistemic: About knowledge: what we know and how we come to know it.
glossary.accountability: Being answerable for a claim, including explaining what it rests on and responding when challenged.
glossary.tactical urbanism: Quick, small changes people make to public spaces to show how they could work better.
glossary.soft-hit posts: Roadside posts used to mark off space that give way when hit instead of acting like a solid barrier.
glossary.clean-room reverse-engineering: A way to recreate how something works by studying its behavior, without using its original source code.
glossary.cease and desist: A formal legal demand to stop doing something.
glossary.patent infringement: Using an invention covered by someone else’s patent without permission.
glossary.kernel driver: Software that lets an operating system use a computer's hardware.
glossary.Lexicon.framework: An Apple system toolset that reads the dictionaries used by the keyboard.
glossary.bitmask: A compact number that lets software keep several yes-or-no labels at once.
glossary.allowlist: A list of apps or people that are allowed to connect.
glossary.Open Access: A collection made available for people to view and use.
glossary.CC0: A way for a creator to let everyone use a work without needing permission.
glossary.CC BY 4.0: A reuse license that lets people share or change a work if they credit its creator.
glossary.Art Nouveau: A style of art and building from around 1890 to 1910, known for curves and nature-inspired decoration.
glossary.Modernisme: Catalonia’s regional version of Art Nouveau.
glossary.Noucentisme: A Catalan movement that replaced Modernisme with a more classical, restrained style.
glossary.trencadís: A mosaic made by setting together irregular pieces of glass.
glossary.vernacular architecture: Buildings made by regular builders without architects designing them.
glossary.payload capacity: The heaviest thing a robot can carry while doing its job.
glossary.fiducial tags: Markers a robot can spot with its camera to recognize a place or object.
glossary.inverse kinematics: Working out how a robot's joints need to move to put its hand at a chosen spot.
glossary.color-scheme: A page setting that tells browsers whether the page supports light mode, dark mode, or both.
glossary.CSS: Cascading Style Sheets: rules that control how a web page looks.
glossary.HTML: HyperText Markup Language: code that tells a browser what content a web page has.
glossary.SVG: Scalable Vector Graphics: a picture format that stays sharp when resized.
glossary.canvas: A webpage area where code can draw pictures or other visuals.
glossary.contrast ratio: A number comparing how different text and background colors look, used to judge readability.
glossary.WCAG: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines: recommendations for making web content easier for people with disabilities to use.
glossary.fingerprinting: Using clues from a device and browser to recognize them without relying on a saved cookie.
glossary.off-balance-sheet debt: Money a company is committed to pay that is not listed among its usual debts.
glossary.RPO: Remaining Performance Obligations: money customers have committed to pay for work the company still has to deliver.
glossary.CapEx: Capital expenditures: money a company spends on long-lasting things it needs, like buildings and equipment.
glossary.AGI: Artificial General Intelligence: a hypothetical AI that could handle many kinds of tasks, not just one narrow job.
glossary.generative model: A program that learns patterns in examples so it can make new examples like them.
glossary.PCA: Principal component analysis: a way to simplify data by keeping its biggest patterns.
glossary.probabilistic PCA: A version of PCA that represents patterns with probabilities, not just fixed values.
glossary.variational autoencoder: A model that learns to make new examples by compressing examples and then recreating them.
glossary.diffusion model: An image-making AI that starts with visual noise and gradually turns it into a picture.
glossary.normalising flow: A model that makes new examples by changing random inputs through steps that can be undone.
glossary.autoregressive factorisation: A way to describe a sequence by predicting each next piece from the pieces before it.
glossary.GAN: Generative adversarial network: a setup where one AI makes examples and another tries to spot fakes.
glossary.Wasserstein GAN: A kind of GAN that judges how different made-up examples are from real ones.
glossary.energy-based model: A model that scores possible examples, with lower scores meaning a better fit.
glossary.linear algebra: A kind of math used to describe how shapes move and turn.
glossary.Algo fatigue: Feeling tired of recommendation feeds deciding what you should watch or read.
glossary.API: Application Programming Interface: a way for one program to ask another for information or actions.
glossary.sideloadable: An app you install on a device yourself, instead of getting it through the device's usual app store.
glossary.BrightScript/SceneGraph: Roku's language and app-building tools for making apps that run on Roku devices.
glossary.vibe coding: Making software by telling an AI what you want and letting it write the code, often without closely checking how it works.
glossary.HOT: Heap Only Tuple: a way to update a database row without changing its lookup lists, when no searched column changes and the new row stays on the same page.
glossary.tuple: A single row of data in a database.
glossary.WAL: Write-ahead log: a record of changes the database saves so it can recover or copy them.
glossary.TOAST: The Oversized-Attribute Storage Technique: a PostgreSQL feature for storing very large values separately from the main row.
glossary.MVCC: Multi-Version Concurrency Control: a way to keep different copies of a row so people can use the database at the same time.
glossary.DIS: The penultimate stage in the ISO standard process; the C++26 draft failed to get enough votes at this stage.
glossary.WG21: C++ Standardization Committee: the group that discusses and votes on proposed changes to C++.
glossary.NB: National Body: a country-level group that votes on proposed ISO standards.
glossary.Contracts: A way to write expectations about what a function should receive or do, so they can be checked.
glossary.formal methods: Ways to check software against precise rules, rather than relying only on trying it out.
glossary.multi-WAN: A setup that can use more than one internet connection.
glossary.uplink: A connection from a device out to the internet or another network.
glossary.dynamic routing: A network automatically picks a path for information based on which routes are available.
glossary.failover: A backup system taking over automatically when the main one stops working.
glossary.load balancing: Spreading traffic across connections so one connection does not have to handle it all.
glossary.firewall rules: Settings that decide which network connections are allowed in or out.
glossary.VPN: Virtual private network: a service that sends your internet traffic through another computer, often to protect it or make it appear to come from somewhere else.
glossary.Jimi Halloween: A Japanese Halloween tradition where people dress as mundane everyday situations.
glossary.API token: A secret code that lets another app or person access a service.
glossary.credentials: The username and password that let someone sign in to an account.
glossary.Git Sync: A way to keep GitBook pages and a Git project updated together.
glossary.MCP server: Model Context Protocol server: a computer that lets an AI connect to outside tools or information.
glossary.post mortem: A report written after an incident to explain what happened and what should change.
glossary.teleprompter: A screen that shows someone the words they’re meant to say while speaking.
glossary.IrDA: Infrared Data Association: a group whose name is used for rules that let nearby devices send information with infrared light.
